content: 1. If postpartum contacts and contacts during the immunization of infants are utilized to deliver rubella-containing vaccines (RCV) to women of reproductive age (WRA), the target population can be estimated as approximately 3% of the total population per year for rough calculations. However, more precise estimates can be achieved by using the country’s birth rate. 2. According to the multi-dose vial policy, once a measles or measles-rubella (MR) vaccine vial has been reconstituted, it must be discarded either at the end of the immunization session or within six hours of opening, whichever occurs first. 3. Each vaccine product sheet should be consulted on the World Health Organization (WHO) prequalification website, specifically referencing the section titled “Handling of opened multi-dose vials.” 4. The introduction of any new vaccine, including a switch to MR-containing vaccines (MRCV), provides an opportunity to critically review and improve the cold chain and logistics (CCL) system. Countries are advised to conduct an Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) assessment and develop a CCL improvement plan. 5. Cold chain challenges are anticipated during vaccination campaigns, particularly if there is a change in vial size or the introduction of a two-dose schedule. Each vaccine storage site must be assessed to ensure adequate capacity. If space is insufficient, decisions must be made regarding the acquisition of additional equipment or alternative mechanisms. 6. The CCL improvement plan should be developed at least one year before the introduction of a new vaccine or campaign to allow for the expansion of the cold chain, including the ordering and installation of cold chain equipment. 7. The commonly used 10-dose MR vaccine presentation is similar in packed volume to the 10-dose measles-only vaccine. If the vial size remains unchanged, introducing rubella as a combination vaccine (MR) in the routine immunization program is a straightforward vial replacement within the existing cold chain and logistics system. 8. Introducing MRCV must be accompanied by efforts to vaccinate WRA and health workers, which may impact cold chain capacity requirements. However, the cold chain capacity for a two-dose MRCV schedule may already exist, depending on the national situation. 9. Adequate dry storage must be available to accommodate additional injection materials, such as syringes (including reconstitution syringes) and safety boxes. Waste management plans must be updated to address the increased volume of used needles and syringes. 10. MRCV should be stored between +2°C and +8°C. The diluent should be refrigerated or kept in a cold box or vaccine carrier at least the night before use to ensure a temperature below +8°C. Reconstituted vaccines should be kept on reconditioned ice packs or in a foam pad hole and discarded after six hours or at the end of the immunization session, whichever comes first. 11. Reconstituted vaccines do not contain preservatives and are susceptible to microbial contamination. Only the diluent provided by the manufacturer should be used for reconstitution to avoid severe adverse events. This must be emphasized during training and supervision. 12. Reconstituted measles and MR vaccines are less stable than the dry powder form and lose potency quickly, especially at room temperatures. At 22°C to 25°C, they lose approximately 50% potency within one hour. They are also sensitive to UV light and must be protected from sunlight. 13. The introduction of MRCV into the routine childhood vaccination program should follow a wide-age-range MRCV vaccination campaign. Logistical challenges for MR campaigns are similar to those for measles-only campaigns, but the wide age range adds extra strain on the cold chain system. 14. The storage and transport needs for MR campaigns are calculated based on the maximum volume of the planned vaccine presentation. Cold chain storage requirements are determined by multiplying the total vaccine required by the packed volume per dose. 15. Passive containers, such as cold boxes and vaccine carriers, will be used for short-term vaccine storage during campaigns. This strategy relies on frequent vaccine distribution using reliable transportation. 16. A communication plan must be developed before introducing any new vaccine, including RCV. Preparatory activities should include establishing a communication committee, coordinating roles among partners, and collecting research to develop an evidence-based communication plan. 17. Key communication messages include the safety of the rubella vaccine for children and adults, its effectiveness in preventing birth defects associated with rubella infection during pregnancy, and its routine administration in combination with the measles vaccine as MR. 18. Health workers must be trained before introducing RCV into the national program. Training should cover operational issues, hands-on practice, and the importance of using the manufacturer-provided diluent to avoid adverse events. 19. School entry screening offers an excellent opportunity to ensure high coverage with RCV and MCV. Children missing doses should be referred to the nearest health facility or vaccinated at school if feasible. 20. Informed consent for vaccination must be obtained from parents or caregivers, as school-aged children are often not legally able to provide consent. Parents and children should be adequately informed about the benefits and risks of measles and rubella vaccinations.
